newsitem.title: USA: Technology key for CME future, exchange head says.
newsitem.headline: Technology key for CME future, exchange head says.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange aims to focus on technology in an effort to compete in the rapidly changing futures markets, but it has some work to do in that area, CME president and chief executive officer Rick Kilcollin said Wednesday.
"Frankly, I think, we've got some catch-up to do, especially in the area of floor technology," Kilcollin told a Futures Industry Association luncheon group. "We're in a very competitive market."
Kilcollin took over as president and CEO of the exchange in February.

"This aspect of competition is pervasive -- the room for error is now much smaller than it was 15 years ago," Kilcollin said. "But there is tremendous potential, unlimited potential for gaining business, if we can remain competitive."
To that end, Kilcollin said last week, the exchange had approved a new policy to "unfetter" member firms to develop and use their own technology on the trading floor.
Under the policy, CME members and member firms can deploy whatever technology they believe can best enhance open outcry markets.

In other developments, Kilcollin was upbeat about a recent deal between Charles Schwab & Co and Chicago futures brokerage Lind-Waldock & Co that would allow some Schwab customers to trade futures through Lind-Waldock.
"I think that's perhaps a signal of things to come and a positive development for the industry," Kilcollin said.

He noted cooperative efforts were under way with the CME's longtime cross-town rival the Chicago Board of Trade. He said the two exchanges were actively pursuing a "common switch," a standardized trading interface for pit and overnight trading.
But discussions about a common clearing endeavor between the two exchanges were "tortured, you might say, looking at the history."
The two exchanges have always competed fiercely, but the rivalry does not extend beyond Chicago, Kilcollin said.

"It is completely clear to me that no one outside of Chicago knows the difference between the Chicago Board of Trade and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange," Kilcollin said. "There's very little to be gained from having separate operations and much to be gained by joining."
Kilcollin noted a "renewed commitment this year to push things forward. It's a very important effort, (but) I don't know where it's going to go," he said.
Exchange officials and members of an industry task force to investigate joint initiatives between Chicago exchanges have set no timeline or target dates for common clearing.
Futures commission merchants have clamored for common operations between exchanges in an effort to streamline their back office procedures and cut costs.
